extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, applicants, PTO examiners, and judges evaluating § 101 patent eligibility
extracted.subtask_description: Application of the Alice/Mayo two-step framework to determine whether claimed subject matter is patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, with attention to whether claims are directed to an abstract idea and whether they contain an inventive concept that transforms the abstract idea into a patent-eligible application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alice/Mayo two-step test
rubrics_metrics.description: First, determine whether the claims at issue are directed to a patent-ineligible concept (e.g., an abstract idea). Second, if so, examine the elements of the claim to determine whether it contains an inventive concept sufficient to transform the claimed abstract idea into a patent-eligible application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the Supreme Court's formulation in Alice and Mayo: step one asks whether the claim is 'directed to' an abstract idea; step two asks whether the claim recites additional elements that add 'something more'—an inventive concept. If both steps counsel ineligibility, affirm rejection under § 101.

rubrics_metrics.name: Categories of patent-ineligible abstract ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Abstract ideas include laws of nature, natural phenomena, and abstract intellectual concepts; familiar classes include (1) methods of organizing human activity (such as fundamental economic practices), (2) mental processes, and (3) claims to results rather than to a means of achieving them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating whether a claim is an abstract idea, consider whether it fits into these familiar classes (Alice, Bilski, Mayo, Benson, Interval Licensing). The opinion explicitly lists these three types and uses them to categorize challenged claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus of the claimed advance / 'character as a whole' inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify the 'focus of the claimed advance over the prior art' to determine if the claim's 'character as a whole' is directed to excluded subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look beyond isolated claim elements to the claim as a whole (Affinity Labs, Elec. Power). If the claimed advance is essentially an abstract idea (for example, collection/analysis/display of information), the claim is likely directed to an abstract idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental processes doctrine
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim steps that can be performed in the human mind, or by a human using pen and paper, are mental processes and fall within the abstract-idea category.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the core steps of the claim (e.g., selecting individuals, determining eligibility, making identifications) are things humans routinely do mentally, the claim is directed to an abstract idea (CyberSource, Elec. Power, Affinity Labs). Computer implementation alone does not avoid this if the steps remain essentially mental.

rubrics_metrics.name: Information collection/analysis/display is an abstract idea absent inventive technology
rubrics_metrics.description: Gathering and analyzing information of a specified content and then displaying the results is an abstract idea unless the claim recites a particular assertedly inventive technology for performing those functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that merely collect information from sources, interpret its meaning, and indicate results (even if performed on a computer network) are typically abstract (Elec. Power, FairWarning). To survive § 101, the claim must do more than data gathering/analysis/display on generic computers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvement to computer functionality vs. generic computer implementation
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that recite an improvement in the functioning of the computer itself (a specific technical solution) can supply an inventive concept; by contrast, claims that use generalized steps on a generic computer are not saved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish claims that 'improve[] an existing technological process' or 'recite a specific, discrete implementation' (BASCOM, Enfish) from those that merely use generic computer components to perform conventional steps (TLI, buySAFE). Emphasize concrete technical improvement over invoking computer capabilities as a tool.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive concept requirement at step two
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim must contain an inventive concept—a claim element or combination of elements that is sufficient to transform the claimed abstract idea into a patent-eligible application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The inventive concept cannot be met by 'stating an abstract idea while adding the words ‘apply it with a computer.’' Look for a 'specific limitation or combination of limitations that are not well-understood, routine, conventional activity' (Alice, Mayo, BASCOM). Mere instructions to perform abstract steps on generic computer hardware are insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Well-understood, routine, conventional elements do not supply an inventive concept
rubrics_metrics.description: Additional claim elements that are well-understood, routine, and conventional in the field do not provide the 'something more' required at Alice/Mayo step two.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the specification or record admits the conventional nature of the computer elements; if so, those elements cannot supply an inventive concept (Alice; Berkheimer: where the specification admits conventionality, relying on the specification may be appropriate).

rubrics_metrics.name: Insignificant extra-solution activity / primitive computer operations
rubrics_metrics.description: Steps that amount to data gathering, data output, or other routine input/output operations on a computer are 'insignificant extra-solution activity' or 'primitive computer operations' and do not render a claim patent-eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be wary of claims that tack on generic operations (providing a processor, storing a record, generating a display) as these are often insufficient to transform an abstract idea into a practical application (Katz, Electric Power, Killian decision).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims directed to results without limiting means (preemption concern)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that 'simply demand[] the production of a desired result . . . without any limitation on how to produce that result' are directed to an abstract idea and raise preemption concerns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the claim preempts all ways of achieving the result; absence of limitations about how the result is achieved points toward ineligibility (Interval Licensing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of specification admissions and record evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Admissions in the specification that steps may be performed on any generic computer or that components are conventional can support a finding that claims lack an inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where the specification concedes that claimed computer components/operations are well-understood, routine, and conventional, that can supply substantial evidence for § 101 rejection without further proof (citing the application's own admission and Berkheimer commentary). Conversely, when non-conventional technical detail is present in the record, it may support eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard of review and evidentiary posture
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent eligibility under § 101 is a question of law that may involve underlying issues of fact: the court reviews the Board's legal conclusions de novo and reviews underlying factual findings for substantial evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating § 101 appeals, apply de novo review to the legal determination and substantial-evidence review to factual findings (e.g., whether elements are conventional). Parties should preserve and present record evidence if contending elements are non-routine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use precedent and common-law comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts decide § 101 questions by comparing the claimed invention to prior Supreme Court and Federal Circuit precedent rather than by invoking a single inflexible rule for 'abstract idea' or 'inventive concept.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify meaningful distinctions (or lack thereof) between the present claim and prior cases (Diehr, Benson, Bilski, Alice, Electric Power, FairWarning, etc.). The common-law method of analogy to prior decisions is the accepted approach to resolve § 101 issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental steps doctrine remains good law
rubrics_metrics.description: The doctrine that mental steps fall within the abstract-idea category continues to be recognized: steps that can be done mentally remain ineligible absent additional inventive features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diehr did not overrule the mental steps doctrine; decisions like Benson, Mayo, and subsequent Federal Circuit precedent treat mental processes as patent-ineligible unless integrated with an inventive technical implementation.
